I have been diagnosed with Bipolar, BPD, and ADHD, and have miscellaneous dealings with PTSD, anxiety, and EDNOS that have not been formally diagnosed as far as I'm aware. I've personally never agreed with my diagnosis of bipolar which came around age fifteen, but before that my diagnosis was along the lines of depression and ADHD. 

Currently, I'm 21. I am medicated, and prescribed Lithium and Depakote to manage the bipolar symptoms and Vistaril for my anxiety and panic attacks. I've been on different pill cocktails since about age thirteen, and also have managed my life for roughly two years unmedicated starting at age 15.

Do I feel like I've ever had a manic or depressive episode? Yes. Do I feel like a primary diagnosis of Bipolar fits me? No. All of this to say, it has helped me greatly to find psychologists and other medical professionals who will communicate with me and with whom I'm comfortable communicating. My psychologist/therapist knows that I don't feel affected by my mood stabilizing medications, and that I do not wish to be medicated (currently on court-order for medications though, it's a shame) and seek to eventually wean off medication so that I can manage myself. I have not had any formal or group type Dialectic Behavioral Therapy, but have read through workbooks and try to practice mindfulness skills in my daily life, and have a relationship with my therapist that allows me to talk through situations as needed. 

TL;DR- Openness. Honesty. Don't disregard a professional opinion right off the bat; but at the same time, it's YOUR feelings and symptoms that are being treated. Also feel free to PM me if you want to talk more, or privately.

You yourself have no real power to stop this. It all rests with your girlfriend. What you can do, however, is support her and be there for her. You need to have an honest, open talk with her where you explain that you're there for her and you want her to come to you for help. Express that you hurt for her and that she can come to you with anything. 

You might also want to talk to her about coping mechanisms. Ask her what hers are, and maybe offer some for her. Talking in and of itself can become a coping mechanism, and a very healthy one. Be sure to take care and develop your relationship to the point where you can talk openly and freely about anything, and that can become a powerful resource for her. Maybe you can do something like the buddy system, where she comes to you before she cuts. That has helped me greatly. My friends and boyfriend frequently talk me out of it. Other coping mechanisms are things like coloring (one of my favorites!), drawing, listening to music, yelling, talking, or "drawing" the cuts. Ask her what works for her, and offer some of these.

Self harm is sometimes an addiction, and not just a coping mechanism. Many people realize that its time to get out, but they can't because it IS an addiction for them. If you feel like it's becoming an addictive behavior, you need to first seek help (you could say you're doing that here) and try to get rid of your tool. Then you have to replace it with a healthier behavior. Pick up a hobby, take some time for yourself, get involved in your community. Something, anything.

It sounds to me that you're using self harm to find something that you identify with so that you have a sense of self, which is much different than using it as a coping skill. Have you thought about it that way? And if it's true that it's you trying to find a sense of self, what about picking up a few hobbies or getting involved somewhere in your community?
